metadata.methods_description: The experiment had an optimization part and a validation part. In the optimization part, four strategies (AUC-ucb, AUC-rand, P300-ucb, P300-rand) each had 20 minutes to find an optimal SOA. In the validation part, the resulting SOAs and a fixed 60 ms SOA were tested with 20 trials each. EEG was recorded with a BrainProducts BrainAmp DC and passive Ag/AgCl electrodes, referenced to the nose. Features were mean amplitudes in 5 time intervals across 31 channels and were classified with shrinkage rLDA using 13-fold cross-validation.

citation_details.title: Adversarial Neural Network Training for Secure and Robust Brain-to-Brain Communication
citation_details.author: Hossein Ahmadi, Ali Kuhestani, Luca Mesin
citation_details.abstract: In the rapidly evolving domain of brain-to-brain communication, safeguarding the transmission of information against adversarial threats is paramount. This study introduces an advanced approach to enhance the resilience and security of brain-to-brain communication systems utilizing electroencephalogram data against such threats through adversarial neural network training. Concentrating on event-related potentials and employing a diverse collection of eight datasets, our research rigorously evaluates and optimizes the system’s defense mechanisms against adversarial manipulations. We specifically target the optimization of trial durations and sampling rates to bolster system security. Our findings reveal a marked improvement in the system’s defensive capabilities, demonstrated by a significant increase in adversarial accuracy by 17% and enhancement in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve by 0.12 points. citation_details.title: Universal semantic feature extraction from EEG signals: a task-independent framework
citation_details.author: Hossein Ahmadi, Luca Mesin
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Objective. Extracting universal, task-independent semantic features from electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains an open challenge. Traditional approaches are often task-specific, limiting their generalization across different EEG paradigms. This study aims to develop a robust, unsupervised framework for learning high-level, task-independent neural representations. Approach. We propose a novel framework integrating convolutional neural networks, AutoEncoders, and Transformers to extract both low-level spatiotemporal patterns and high-level semantic features from EEG signals. The model is trained in an unsupervised manner to ensure adaptability across diverse EEG paradigms, including motor imagery (MI), steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs), and event-related potentials (ERPs, specifically P300). Extensive analyses, including clustering, correlation, and ablation studies, are conducted to validate the quality and interpretability of the extracted features. Main

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.
